name: Asparagus
lede: Asparagus is a mid-light yellowish green named for the vegetable, and as a color word it is older than most people expect: it sits at number 58 in Werner's list of mineral colors as Syme published it in Britain.

sections.title: A vegetable's name
sections.body: Paterson's dictionary defines *asparagus* simply as the green of the vegetable, also written *asparagus-green* [1]. St Clair's glossary of other interesting colors describes it as a toned-down spring green [2]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary of color gives 1805 as the first recorded use of the name, which makes it a nineteenth-century word, not a modern food-court one [3].

sections.title: Number 58 in Werner's list
sections.body:
The mineralogist Abraham Gottlob Werner's list of colors, made for describing minerals and published in Britain by Patrick Syme, gives asparagus green the number 58 among the greens [4]. Syme defined it as pistachio green mixed with much greyish white [4]. In the same list [[pistachio]] is emerald green with a little lemon yellow and some brown, [[sap-green]] is emerald with much saffron yellow, and [[olive-green]] is grass green with much brown [4].

Syme's list gave each color three examples, one from the animal, vegetable and mineral kingdoms. For asparagus green they are the brimstone butterfly, the leaves of a variegated horseshoe geranium, and beryl [4]. Beryl is the mineral family that includes [[gem:emerald|emerald]] [4]. A modern edition illustrates them with a butterfly plate from 1782, a flower plate from 1857 and a mineral plate from 1916 [4].

The name was not Syme's alone [5]. It appears in the 108-color list of Syme's 1814 edition and in the 80-color list printed by the American mineralogist Parker Cleaveland in 1816, which Baty says is almost identical to the one in Jameson's 1805 book, itself based on Werner [5][6].

sections.title: Which asparagus
sections.body: The swatch on this page, #77AB56, is the color that web surveys settled on in 2010: a moderate yellow green, block 120 in the ISCC-NBS system [7]. It is not Werner's [4][7]. The library's *Asparagus Green*, drawn from Werner, Maerz and Paul and Ridgway, is a pale greyish yellow-green, #C2C190, about 31 units of Lab distance away from this swatch [7]. Both are called asparagus, but one is a paint-box green and the other is the washed, greyed green that Syme described in words [4][7]. The aged chart swatch may have faded, so treat the older number as approximate [7]. The older color has its own page, [[asparagus-green]].

sections.title: Asparagus and sap green
sections.body: The vegetable shows up in pigment history by an odd route. Sap green, a paint made from plant juice, is colored almost entirely by chlorophyll, according to Mills and White, so it could be made from many leaves and berries [8]. An early seventeenth-century Portuguese treatise by Nunes names asparagus seeds among the possible sources, which the Pigment Compendium cites as an example of that variety [8]. It is a single mention, and the book does not say that anyone made a lasting paint this way [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, 13 contain this green as at least five per cent of the canvas, within a ΔE of 6 [9]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a screen reading and not a pigment test [9]. The largest cover is a portrait of Emperor Jahangir dated 1795 in the museum record, where it fills 51 per cent [9]. Next come Matisse's [[painting:commons-Q21723020|Nymph and Satyr]] of 1908 and Morisot's [[painting:nga-52194|Girl in a Boat with Geese]] of 1889, each around 32 per cent [9].

The color is almost absent before 1800 and then turns up in the nineteenth century: 7 of 8,345 paintings from the 1800s, and 4 of 1,674 from the 1900s, about four times the average rate [9]. Two of the 168 Mughal paintings hold it, a lift of about 22 times, and one of 140 Impressionist paintings does too [9]. Van Gogh's [[painting:nga-163323|Green Wheat Fields, Auvers]] of 1890 reaches 16 per cent [9]. When it appears it is a lit color, with 62 per cent of its pixels in the highlight band [9].

Google Books shows *asparagus* peaking around 1931, but the word is overwhelmingly the vegetable, so that curve says little about the color [10].

questions.q: In Syme's version of Werner's list, what is asparagus green?
choices: Pistachio green mixed with much greyish white
Olive green with a little blue
questions.answer: Pistachio green mixed with much greyish white

questions.q: True or false: the asparagus green of Werner's list is the same bright green as the swatch on this page.
Which mineral did Syme give as the mineral example of asparagus green?

openers: Asparagus green was number 58 on a mineralogist's list of colors, published in Britain by Syme.
Werner's asparagus green is a washed, greyish tint; the web's asparagus is much brighter.
